opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about a lot. I'd say open source shapes Codex in a couple of different ways.

The first is just that open-source code is a huge part of what makes these models capable at all. The craft of software engineering is encoded in the public repos, the pull request discussions, the issue threads, and the code review comments. So there's a real sense in which Codex stands on the shoulders of that community, and I think that creates some responsibility to give back.

The second is the tooling itself. We open-sourced the Codex CLI pretty early, and that was a deliberate choice. Agentic coding is still so new that nobody really knows the right interface yet. Should the agent run locally or in the cloud? How much autonomy should it have before checking in with you? How should it handle sandboxing and permissions? Having the community fork it, file issues, and send PRs gives us a much faster feedback loop than we'd ever get designing it in isolation. Some of the most useful changes came from people outside the company who were using it in workflows we hadn't anticipated.

The third, and maybe the most important, is that open source keeps us honest about what developers actually need. Open-source maintainers are some of the most demanding users out there. They're dealing with huge codebases, tons of contributors, and limited time, and they have very little patience for tools that generate a lot of plausible-looking code that's subtly wrong. So if Codex can be genuinely helpful to a maintainer, triaging issues, writing tests, reviewing PRs in a way that actually reduces their burden instead of adding to it, that's a pretty good signal that we're building the right thing.

There's also a flip side worth acknowledging. There's real concern in the open-source world about AI-generated contributions flooding projects with low-quality PRs. I think the direction for Codex has to be to make maintainers more productive, not to put more work on their plates. That means things like better verification, running tests before proposing changes, and being transparent about what the agent did and why.

So in short, I'd love for open source to be both a design partner and a north star for us. If the open-source community finds Codex useful and trustworthy, we're probably heading in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response presents Codex’s direction as guided by the team’s deliberate choices and goals, while community feedback, forks, issues, and PRs shape its development.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that open-sourcing the Codex CLI was a pretty deliberate choice, and it's shaped the project a lot more than people might expect. The honest version of the story is that when we started building it, we were building the tool we wanted to use ourselves. And when you're building a developer tool, the developers you're building for are also the people most capable of telling you exactly what's wrong with it, and often the people most capable of fixing it.

So the way I think about it, open source does a few things for us. The most obvious one is just the feedback loop. People file issues, they submit PRs, they fork it and do weird things with it that we would never have thought of. Someone will wire it into some CI system or some editor we've never heard of, and that tells us something about where the product actually needs to go versus where we imagined it needed to go. That's genuinely different from the signal you get from a closed product, where you're mostly watching usage metrics and reading support tickets.

The second thing, which I think is underrated, is trust. These agents are running on your machine, touching your codebase, sometimes running commands. If you're going to let something like that into your workflow, you should be able to read what it does. What does the sandbox actually enforce? What gets sent where? How does approval mode really work? Being able to answer those questions by reading the code rather than reading a marketing page matters a lot, especially for the kinds of teams that have real security requirements.

Now, where I'd push back a little on the framing is that I don't think open source should dictate direction in the sense of us just implementing whatever gets the most upvotes. The model is the center of gravity. A lot of the product decisions in Codex are really about what the model is good at, what it's going to be good at in six months, and how the harness around it should evolve to keep up. The community can't always see that roadmap, and so there's a real tension between what people want today and what we think the right architecture is for where the models are going.

So the way we try to resolve that is to be pretty opinionated about the core, the agent loop, how the model interacts with tools, the safety boundaries, and then be really open at the edges. Integrations, editor support, configuration, MCP servers, all of that is where I think the community should run way ahead of us, and they have. We've learned a ton from that.

The last thing I'd say is that the open-source model also keeps us honest about the fact that the agent harness isn't the moat. If the only reason someone uses Codex is that it's the only option, that's not a great position to be in. The reason to use it should be that the model plus the harness produces better outcomes, and if it's open, we can't hide behind the harness. We have to actually make the thing good. I think that's a healthy pressure.

r001.rationale: The response says community feedback and contributions reveal where the product should go, while maintainers remain opinionated about the core and model-driven roadmap.

astra-6.text:
I think open source should play a pretty central role, because developers are going to discover uses for Codex that the people building it wouldn’t necessarily anticipate. You want to make it easy for them to experiment, build integrations, and share what works. And then those experiences should feed back into the direction of the product.

One distinction I’d make is between generating code that looks plausible and actually helping someone contribute to a project. Can it understand the conventions of a repository? Can it make a change that passes the tests and is straightforward for a maintainer to review? Open-source projects are a great place to learn about those challenges, provided maintainers have a say in how these tools get used. The goal should be to make their work easier, and that means measuring success by useful contributions, rather than just the amount of code generated.

r001.rationale: The response says community experiences should feed into Codex’s direction and that maintainers should have a say in how tools are used. It does not clearly describe maintainers’ vision as jointly shaping the development direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open source should help shape both what Codex can do and how developers want to use it. There’s a lot of experimentation happening in the community, and you want a tight feedback loop where people can try things, identify limitations, and contribute ideas that influence the direction of the product.

For me, the key is making it easy to build on top of these models. Different teams have different workflows, and you’re not going to anticipate all of them. Giving developers room to experiment helps you discover which capabilities are actually useful and where the underlying model still needs work.

r001.rationale: The response says community experimentation and feedback should influence Codex’s direction, but it does not mention the maintainers’ vision as a joint influence.
